content.title: How NASA plans to send humans farther into space than ever before | National Geographic
content.text: > mexico facebook twitter instagram subscribe RETURN TO THE MOON Back to the moon NASA’s latest lunar missions are also preparing for deep‑space exploration well beyond our closest neighbor. By ALBERTO LUCAS LÓPEZ, RONALD PANIAGUA, and RYAN MORRIS Updated Jan. 13, 2026 NASA’s newest spacecraft is designed to carry humans not only to the moon but farther into space than ever before. The multi-mission Artemis project’s first journey, in 2022, saw the uncrewed Artemis I Orion spacecraft venture thousands of miles beyond the moon and successfully return to Earth. Next up: Artemis II will launch from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center as soon as February 2026 with four astronauts on board. They’ll be propelled into flight by NASA’s evolvable, super heavy-lift SLS (Space Launch System) rocket for a 10-day mission around the far side of the moon. The aim: to put systems and astronauts through their paces to prepare for future missions, pushing the boundaries of deepspace exploration to the moon and beyond.
